newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: FOCUS-The bugbear of broken quotas plagues OPEC.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-The bugbear of broken quotas plagues OPEC.

text.p: OPEC ministers gathered in Vienna for talks that will have to confront the violations of their cartel quotas that threaten to send world oil prices skidding to the bargain basement again.

An early arrival for a conference that opens on Wednesday was the minister of Iran, Gholamreza Aqazadeh, who has called for discipline among the 11 fractious members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC).
"We have overproduction...stop violations," he said, when questioned by lobby reporters.

At the opposite pole, however, the state oil company of Venezuela, a country that is exceeding its mandatory volume, has said OPEC should scrap quotas altogether and bid for bigger market share instead.

The divisions lie at the heart of a debate about OPEC's future, say market analysts, who also do not see much prospect of a reduction of some two million barrels per day of OPEC supply in excess of an agreed limit of 25.03 million.

Low stocks, cold weather and delays to resumed Iraqi oil sales late in 1996 had lifted prices to post-Gulf War highs around $25 per barrel. But the oil companies have replenished their stocks and prices are now around $18.

Even so, delegates doubted if OPEC would do more than nod through a further extension of current quotas, with some pious words from its compliance committee which meets on Tuesday ahead of the conference itself.
Venezuela's Erwin Arrieta, alleged by monitors to be above quota by 800,000 barrels a day, was an early arrival.

He said "No" when lobby reporters asked if he would press at this meeting to scrap quotas altogether. But he added that "we want to widen the spectrum to consider other aspects...We want to find spaces where there will be room for all producers"
That appeared to be a reference to a Venezuelan plan to restructure OPEC on regional lines in a way that would, in effect, free Venezuela to sell as much as it wanted to the United States.
OPEC linchpin Saudi Arabia is cool to that idea and Western industry officials believe it is a non-starter.

The Saudis, who have a huge quota of 8.0 million barrels, with Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates, form a core of big Gulf Arab sellers who support oil prices by adhering to quotas and do not seem to favour a free-for-all.

But the Venezuelan state oil company, Petroleos de Venezuela, which has called for OPEC to abandon quotas and boost revenue by increasing market share, says it hopes to pump 4.0 million barrels daily in 1999.
At that volume, up from 3.2 million now, it could take a 10 percent drop in prices and still increase revenue.
Nigeria, facing internal fuel shortages despite its own crude oil production, is another cash-strapped Third World seller that is exceeding its quota.
These divisions seem to stymie OPEC.

Peter Gignoux, head of the London energy desk at Smith Barney, pointed on Monday to present delays over further U.N.-supervised Iraqi oil sales as a more potent factor in support of prices than the activities of the cartel.
Benchmark IPE Brent crude ended Monday in London up 33 cents at $18 in a rush of late buying in a market that participants said was concerned by tensions between Iraq and the United Nations.
